w: The Casa das Historias Paula Rego, its name meaning House of Stories, is a museum in Cascais on the Portuguese Riviera. It was purpose-built, designed by the architect Eduardo Souto de Moura, to house the work of the painter Paula Rego, who lived from 1935 to 2022.
s: A museum built solely to house Paula Rego's work
_facts: Museum in Cascais housing works by painter Paula Rego (1935-2022)
Designed by architect Eduardo Souto de Moura

w: Once the citadel governor's residence, this palace inside the Citadel of Cascais became the royal family's summer home, visited every September from 1870 until King Carlos I's 1908 assassination. Later used by presidents, it fell into neglect before reopening as a museum in 2011, part of the Museum of the Presidency.
s: Where Portugal's royals summered every September
_facts: Former governor's residence inside the Citadel of Cascais
Royal summer residence every September from 1870 to 1908
Restored and reopened as a museum in 2011

w: South of central Cascais, this quadrangular masonry lighthouse guides ships into Cascais Bay and the town's marina at the mouth of the Tagus, its white-tiled tower banded in blue with a red lantern. Built on the grounds of the old Santa Marta Fort, which now houses a lighthouse museum.
_facts: Quadrangular white-tiled tower with blue stripes and red lantern
Built on the grounds of Santa Marta Fort
Fort now houses a lighthouse museum

w: Built in 1900 as a summer residence and originally called the Torre de Sao Sebastiao, this eclectic-style palace in Cascais became a museum in 1931. Its collection spans paintings of national and international significance, plus furniture, porcelain, jewellery, and a neo-Gothic organ.
s: A 1900 tower turned museum of art and porcelain
_facts: Built 1900 as summer residence, originally Torre de Sao Sebastiao
Became a museum in 1931
Eclectic architectural style; collection of paintings, furniture, porcelain

w: Designed by the Portuguese architect Raul Lino, Casa de Santa Maria is a historic house museum on the Portuguese Riviera in Cascais. It stands as a textbook example of both the region's Summer architecture and Lino's own Casa Portuguesa school.
s: Raul Lino's own house museum school
_facts: Historic house museum designed by architect Raul Lino
Example of Portuguese Summer architecture and Lino's Casa Portuguesa school

n: Fort of Santo António da Barra
w: Overlooking the sea in Estoril, this fort is sometimes called the Old Fort, or the Fort of Salazar, after dictator Antonio de Oliveira Salazar, who used it as his seasonal residence. Left disused and vandalised for years, it was restored by the municipality and opened to the public on 25 April 2018.
s: Salazar's seaside fort, reopened after decades
_facts: Also known as the Old Fort or Fort of Salazar
Used as Salazar's seasonal residence during the dictatorship
Restored and opened to the public on 25 April 2018

w: Four subterranean tombs carved into marlstone rock with stone tools make up this prehistoric necropolis in the centre of Alapraia, a suburb of Estoril within Cascais. The hypogea are believed to date to the last quarter of the 4th millennium BCE and to have served as a burial site for more than a thousand years.
s: Prehistoric tombs cut into Alapraia's rock
_facts: Four subterranean tombs (hypogea) carved from marlstone
Dated to the last quarter of the 4th millennium BCE
Used as a necropolis for over a thousand years

w: Also known as the Fort of Velas, this fort sits at the edge of Praia do Abano near Guincho, in the parish of Alcabideche. Declared a Property of Public Interest in 1977, it stands today in a state of decay, despite studies to convert it into a visitor centre for the Sintra-Cascais Nature Park.
s: A decaying fort at the edge of Guincho's dunes
_facts: Also known as the Fort of Velas
Property of Public Interest since 1977
Currently decayed; studied as a Sintra-Cascais Nature Park visitor centre

n: Fort of São Jorge at Oitavos
w: Sitting on the coastal highway EN 247 near the Oitavos dunes, this fort was one link in a chain of fortifications running from the Tower of Belem near Lisbon all the way to Cabo da Roca. It has since been converted into a museum, one of several coastal forts around Cascais now open to visitors instead of soldiers.
s: One link in a chain of forts to Cabo da Roca
_facts: Located near the Oitavos dunes on highway EN 247
Part of a chain of forts from the Tower of Belem to Cabo da Roca
Now operates as a museum

w: Also called the Fort of Poca for the Estoril beach it sits on, this fort was built between 1642 and 1648, in the Joanine era. It formed part of a defensive line stretching from the Fort of Sao Juliao da Barra to Cabo da Roca, guarding this stretch of the Cascais coast.
s: The fort that guards Estoril's Poca beach
_facts: Also known as the Fort of Poca, on Praia da Poca
Built 1642-1648, Joanino-era fortification
Part of a defensive line from Fort of Sao Juliao da Barra to Cabo da Roca

w: Built in 1762 to defend Cresmina beach from seaborne landings, this fort passed into private ownership in 1889 and, as of 2021, was being converted into a restaurant. Also known as the Fort of Crismina, it sits at the beach's southern end in Cascais municipality, a coastal defence turned dining room.
s: An 18th-century fort, now becoming a restaurant
_facts: Built 1762 to protect Cresmina beach
Privately owned since 1889
Being converted into a restaurant as of 2021

w: Built in 1874 as a summer residence for the Duke and Duchess of Palmela, this palace, also known as the Conceicao Velha, stands in Cascais as a major example of the town's distinctive Summer architecture, the aristocratic building style that flourished here in the late 19th century.
s: A duke and duchess's seaside summer palace
_facts: Built 1874 for the Duke and Duchess of Palmela
Also known as the Conceicao Velha
A major example of Cascais's Summer architecture

n: Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Assunção
w: The Mother Church of Cascais, its exact construction date unknown, carries interior decoration dated to between 1520 and 1525, making it one of the town's oldest surviving buildings. It already appears clearly in a 1572 engraving depicting a view of Cascais from the sea, one of the earliest visual records of the town.
s: Cascais's mother church, painted since the 1520s
_facts: Mother Church of Cascais
Interior decoration dated 1520-1525
Depicted in a 1572 engraving of Cascais seen from the sea

w: The Palacio dos Condes da Guarda now serves as the headquarters of the Municipality of Cascais, its ground floor doubling as a museum on the town's history. A former aristocratic residence turned seat of local government, it is named for its original noble owners, the Counts of Guarda.
s: Noble palace turned town hall and history museum
_facts: Headquarters of the Municipality of Cascais
Ground floor houses a museum on the town's history
Named for its original owners, the Counts of Guarda

w: Built as the residence of entrepreneur Henrique de Sommer, Casa Sommer is a noted example of Cascais's Summer architecture, now repurposed to hold the town's archives. It houses the Cascais Municipal Historical Archive and a branch of the Municipal Library, with collections on local archaeology and history.
s: A Summer-style house now holding the town's memory
_facts: Built as the residence of entrepreneur Henrique de Sommer
Houses the Cascais Municipal Historical Archive and a library branch
Example of Cascais's Summer architecture

w: Founded in 1938, the Clube Naval de Cascais built its name on sailing, hosting numerous world championships over the decades. Its biggest moment came in 2007, staging the ISAF Sailing World Championships, the main qualifying regatta for the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
s: The sailing club that sent racers to Beijing
_facts: Founded 1938, primarily a sailing club
Hosted the 2007 ISAF Sailing World Championships
Was the main qualifying event for the 2008 Olympic Games
